content_list.content_text: During the 1990s, the leading Chinese filmmakers of the Fifth Generation increasingly sought foreign audiences and courted international film festivals, even while facing censorship at home. Zhang Yimou (b. 1951) directed Da Hong Deng Long Gao Gao Gua (Raise the Red Lantern, 1991), which won the Silver Lion at Venice.

information.contentText: Because of its themes, which can be seen as a critique of the United States, the film was praised by North Korean authorities, a rarity for a South Korean hit.

content_list.content_text: With the Palme d'Or winner Ba Wang Bie Ji (Farewell My Concubine, 1993), Chen Kaige (b. 1952) traced the relationship between two Peking Opera stars through the Cultural Revolution. Celebrated abroad, these films were temporarily banned in China. The Fifth Generation drew hostility and criticism not only from the state but also from younger filmmakers, who longed for a more direct engagement with modern Chinese reality.

content_list.title: The Visual Poetry of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
content_list.description:
Director Ang Lee said his intention with Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon was simply to make the best martial arts film possible. The artistic success and popularity of the result suggest that he succeeded. Working from a screenplay by his longtime collaborator James Schamus (b. 1959), Lee assembled a cast of Asian action superstars who also had the artistic talent needed to let the story flow.

Lee also made a brilliant decision in recruiting the famous fight choreographer Yuen Woo-ping. Inspired by the physicality of Chinese theater, Yuen defies the laws of physics, hoisting the actors on wires so they can fight atop the trees, skim across water like skipping stones, run up walls and, several times, battle in midair. For Western audiences, perhaps unaccustomed to these aerial ballets, the sight of the opening scene's chase on foot across village rooftops on a moonlit night proved immediately and irresistibly appealing.

Chow Yun-Fat (b. 1955), Michelle Yeoh (b. 1962) and the relative newcomer Zhang Ziyi (b. 1979) handle the supernatural physical demands of their roles with ease, but their performances never fall short of the impressive action scenes. Indeed, one of the reasons Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon became such a sensation was the attention the film paid to plot and character development, two rarities even for the most ambitious martial arts films.

A strongly feminist undercurrent also runs through Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, adding another layer of intelligence. The female characters fight for different reasons, but most of them seem to be fighting for respect in a man's world. Having run away from home, young Zhang, passing herself off as a male warrior, is attacked at an inn by several truculent fighters. Lee turns the inevitable beating she gives dozens of would-be attackers into a joke, a hyperkinetic variation on the old bar brawl. But part of Zhang's passionate response seems to stem from a long-held resentment at believing she would be scorned rather than respected (or feared) as a formidable opponent if they knew she was a woman.

Lee modulates every scene of the film with similar nuance and sensitivity. His fight sequences play out as much as psychological contests as sword fights, with clashes between innocence and experience, peace and rage. Still, Lee leaves room for lightness and visual poetry, striking a rare balance of excitement, beauty, humor and intelligence.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: A notable transitional figure was Xiaowen Zhou (b. 1954), who technically belongs to the Fifth Generation but whose chilling satire Ermo (1994) already showed the engagement with contemporary society that would characterize the next generation.

information.contentText: The film follows the story of a man named Oh Dae-su, who is locked in a hotel room for 15 years without knowing his captors' motive. When he is finally released, Dae-su finds himself caught in a web of conspiracy and violence. His quest for revenge becomes intertwined with a romance when he falls for an attractive sushi chef.

content_list.content_text: The Chinese director with the greatest international impact was Taiwan's Ang Lee (b. 1954), whose first two films, Tui shou (Pushing Hands, 1992) and Xi yan (The Wedding Banquet, 1993), are set in the United States and depict the culture clash between Asia and the West. While other Taiwanese directors such as Edward Yang (1947-2007) made art films, like Yi yi (2000), Lee directed the stylish martial arts film Wo Hu Cang Long (Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, 2000), which inspired Ying Xiong (Hero, 2002) and Shi Mian Mai Fu (House of Flying Daggers, 2004).

These visually splendid epics found eager audiences abroad and sealed the internationalization of East Asian cinema. This can also be seen in the work of Hong Kong director Wong Kar-Wai (b. 1956), who in films such as Hua Yang De Nian Hua (In the Mood for Love, 2000) opted for a so-called "MTV aesthetic," discarding the austerity of Asian art cinema in favor of the style of international commercials and music videos.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
information.contentText: The film was originally written as a five-part novel series by Wang Dulu, starting in the late 1930s. The story presented in the film is adapted and condensed from the plot of the fourth book in the series, Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.

content_list.content_text: While Chinese directors were still wrestling with censorship, South Korean cinema benefited from its liberation from state control in the democratic era. The result was the maturing of the country's filmmaking, which also began to attract international attention. Hong Sang-Soo (b. 1960) was acclaimed by local and foreign critics for his debut film, Daijiga umule pajinnal (The Day a Pig Fell Into the Well, 1996), which tells four loosely interconnected life stories in modern Seoul.

quote.quote: A work that seeks to filter the experience of Taiwan's transition to modernity through the dual lens of romantic relationships and family.
quote.author: Edward Tang on Yi Yi

content_list.content_text: Chan-Wook Park (b. 1963) won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival for Oldboy (2003), a brutal revenge story. Kim Ki-Duk (b. 1960) gained fame and notoriety with the ultraviolent Seom (The Isle, 2000), but later opted for a more serene style with the Buddhist parable Bom Yeoreum Gaeul Gyeoul Geurigo Bom (Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring, 2003).

information.contentText: Miramax Films bought the U.S. distribution rights but delayed the film's release for almost two years, until Quentin Tarantino finally persuaded Miramax to release the film in American theaters in 2004.

content_list.content_text: The success of these films showed the genuine enthusiasm of some Korean audiences for their national cinema. Seopyeonje (Sopyonje, 1993), an underrated melodrama about a family of folk singers directed by Im Kwon-taek (b. 1936), became the most commercially successful Korean film up to that time, but was surpassed in 1999 by Swiri (Shiri, 1999).

content_list.title: The Ultimate Revenge Story
content_list.description:
Mysticism, poetry, school days and a futuristic bedroom are some of the surprises found in Oldboy, a thriller that draws on Oedipal taboos and the blindness of chance, on hypnotism and fate. Part action film, part drama, part psychological thriller, this groundbreaking work introduced South Korean cinema to more viewers than any other. The story is more direct and engaging than that of director Park Chan-Wook's previous film, the popular Boksuneun Naui Geot (Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance, 2002), and it starts explosively. A man is imprisoned for 15 years without any explanation. When he escapes, he has only five days to find those responsible for his incarceration.

This violent, elegiac masterpiece is based on a Japanese manga by Garon Tsuchiya. Actor Choi Min-sik (b. 1962), who did without stunt doubles, trained rigorously for the role of the hapless victim of a mysterious kidnapping. Dae-su manages to escape from his windowless prison and, once free, in the manner of the Count of Monte Cristo, he swears revenge on the jailer who robbed him of his daughter, his wife and his entire life. Transformed into a ragged fighting machine, like a Korean Charles Bronson in a cheap wig, Dae-su befriends a beautiful sushi-bar chef (Hye-Jeong Kang), whose interest he piques by eating a live squid and then passing out face-first on the counter. That is the blockbuster style of Oldboy. But this complex tale is imbued with a clearly unfolding logic, easily incorporating the film's many flashbacks. The pace of the action is breathtaking, but there is also time for thought. The choreographed fights are both innovative and surprising, and all the violence serves the plot.

Despite the prevailing brutality, this is a film that is, at heart, a black comedy that skillfully combines elements of gangster films and revenge thrillers. After winning the Grand Prix at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival, the director stunned the audience by thanking the cast and crew, as well as the four squid that sacrificed their lives for that sushi-bar scene.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Karen Krizanowich, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: That film, in turn, gave up the title of most profitable Korean production of all time to Gwoemul (The Host, 2006), a monster movie with political overtones. Despite globalization, everything suggests that Asian cinema can captivate audiences in its own countries.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Oldboy
movies.overview: With no clue how he came to be imprisoned, drugged and tortured for 15 years, a desperate businessman seeks revenge on his captors.
Two warriors in pursuit of a stolen sword and a notorious fugitive are led to an impetuous, physically-skilled, teenage nobleman's daughter, who is at a crossroads in her life.
movies.title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon

movies.overview: Following the dumping of gallons of toxic waste in the river, a giant mutated squid-like appears and begins attacking the populace. Gang-du's daughter Hyun-seo is snatched up by the creature; with his family to assist him, he sets off to find her.
movies.title: The Host
Hero
movies.overview: One man defeated three assassins who sought to murder the most powerful warlord in pre-unified China.

1986 Gyunggi Province. The body of a young woman is found brutally raped and murdered. Two months later, a series of rapes and murders commences under similar circumstances. And in a country that had never known such crimes, the dark whispers about a serial murderer grow louder. A special task force is set up in the area, with two local detectives Park Doo-Man and Jo Young-Goo joined by a detective from Seoul who requested to be assigned to the case.
movies.title: Memories of Murder
Farewell My Concubine
movies.overview: Abandoned by his prostitute mother in 1920, Douzi was raised by a theater troupe. There he meets Shitou and over the following years the two develop an act entitled "Farewell My Concubine" that brings them fame and fortune. When Shitou marries Juxian, Doutzi becomes jealous, the beginnings of the acting duo's explosive breakup and tragic fall take root.

movies.title: Raise the Red Lantern
movies.overview: China in the 1920s. After her father's death, 19 year old Songlian is forced to marry the much older lord of a powerful family. With three wives already, each living in a separate house within the great castle, there is fierce competition for his attention and the privileges that are gained. This competition gets out of hand...

movies.title: Hua yang de nian hua
movies.overview: Hua yang de nian hua is a 2000 short film by Hong Kong director Wong Kar-wai that was shown at the 2001 Berlin International Film Festival. It consists of a 2m 28s montage of scenes from vintage Chinese films, most of which were considered lost until some nitrate prints were discovered in a California warehouse during the 1990s, set to a song from the soundtrack of Wong’s In the Mood for Love (2000), a golden oldie by Zhou Xuan.

movies.title: Yi Yi
movies.overview: Each member of a family in Taipei asks hard questions about life's meaning as they live through everyday quandaries.

movies.title: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring
movies.original_title: 봄 여름 가을 겨울 그리고 봄
movies.overview: An isolated lake, where an old monk lives in a small floating temple. The monk has a young boy living with him, learning to become a monk. We watch as seasons and years pass by.

movies.title: Sopyonje
movies.overview: Dong-ho, a pansori performer, travels the country in search of Song-hwa, a fellow orphan who also studied under the same strict master.
